title: Playing it hot and waltzes before World War I
summary: He explains what 'play it hot' meant and that bands also had to play waltzes, placing Dixieland's arrival around World War I.

story.theme_name: Playing for dancers: dance bands and the dances themselves
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: What do they mean by play it hot?
They meant play it fast. Play some hot music. Play some hot music.
That's like four beats to a bar?

Yeah. It's fast. Dixieland. They used to like to jump fast, you know, but we wouldn't do that too regularly, now and then. And after we'd play a fast, we would play a waltz. People hardly ever asked for waltz. Back in those times they considered that was a very bad business. There wasn't much of a band if you didn't play a waltz.
When was this? That's before the 20s.
Before? Yeah, the 20s, that's when the Dixieland came in.
You're talking about like before the war, before World War?

Before the war. Before World War I. You see. When World War I come in then the bands, after that the bands start Dixieland music. Dixieland is traditional jazz, the last chorus of traditional jazz, you understand? Where we run into four beats and hit all the drum and the bass hitting boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom. Everything is, that's the, Dixieland is the last part of traditional jazz.
